passage: "Okay, Aadhya, promise you won't laugh. Remember the school trip to the planetarium last Friday? The lights went down, the ceiling filled with stars, and the guide said the light from some of them left before any human was born. I just sat there with goosebumps. Then she told us about a woman in a small town who mapped comets from her rooftop, teaching herself from borrowed books by lamplight. I came home and couldn't sleep. I pulled my old telescope down from the loft, wiped the lens with my dupatta and made a list of constellations to find this month. Three so far. I know, classic dramatic Ayesha 😅 but it felt like someone opened a window in my chest. I want to learn the sky properly now, and not just for marks."

qa.q: Where did Ayesha's class go on the school trip last Friday?
qa.a: They went to the planetarium.

qa.q: What does Ayesha mean when she says it felt like a window opened in her chest?
qa.a: She felt deeply moved and suddenly hopeful; the idea of ancient starlight and the self-taught comet mapper stirred a real wish to learn, which is why she could not sleep and dug out her telescope.

qa.q: How could Aadhya support Ayesha's new interest?
qa.a: Aadhya could take it seriously instead of teasing, ask about the three constellations, or join her on the roof one night to look. 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Ayesha studied the sky only for marks?
qa.a: The spark would likely fade after the exam; because the wonder is her own, she keeps going without anyone asking her to.

grounding: Illustrates a teen being deeply moved by a vast idea and a role model's story, and turning that feeling into motivation.

passage: My sister Aditi used to scroll for hours after school. Then last month her art teacher took the class to watch a mural being painted under the flyover: a huge wall showing the women who sweep our roads at dawn, painted by an artist who once swept roads herself. Aditi came home unusually quiet. She didn't touch her phone that night. Next morning I found her at the dining table with charcoal on her fingers, sketching the aunty who sells vegetables at our gate. Now she carries a sketchbook everywhere. When I asked why, she only said, "Vikas, people walk past them every day and never look." I can't say exactly what shifted inside her. But her eyes go bright whenever that wall comes up, and she has already filled half the book.

qa.q: Where was the mural being painted?
qa.a: It was being painted under the flyover.

qa.q: What does Aditi's line about people never looking suggest she feels?
qa.a: She seems stirred by the idea that ordinary workers deserve to be seen, and the painter's own story makes her want to do the same with her drawing.

qa.q: How could her parents help this new drive last?
qa.a: They could notice and ask about her sketches, keep charcoal and paper around, and maybe take her to see more public art, without turning it into pressure.

qa.q: How does Vikas see the change in Aditi?
qa.a: Vikas is a little puzzled and cannot be sure what changed inside her, but clearly notices and seems to respect her brightness and her filled pages.

grounding: Shows, through a sibling's eyes, a teen motivated by art and an artist's example to make her own work.

passage:
Sunday: Santosh slouched through music class at school, sawing at the cheap violin his parents had bought, and told Yash the whole thing was pointless. "Nobody listens to this stuff anymore."

Wednesday: At Yash's flat, Yash's grandfather put on a crackling old recording of a sarangi player who had lost his sight as a boy and still toured villages for fifty years. Santosh stopped chewing his biscuit. His throat went tight. When it ended, he asked, very quietly, "Can we hear that again?"

Two weeks later: Yash groaned into his phone. "Bro, it's six in the morning and I can hear you from my balcony." Santosh laughed, but he didn't stop. He was trying, for the twentieth time, to copy one sliding phrase from that record.

qa.q: What instrument was Santosh practising two weeks later?
qa.a: He was practising his violin.

qa.q: Why did Santosh ask to hear the recording again?
qa.a: The music and the player's life story moved him deeply; his tight throat and sudden stillness show it touched something his classes never had.

qa.q: What small step could help Santosh turn this feeling into lasting practice?
qa.a: He could ask Yash's grandfather for more recordings or a teacher's name, and keep a short daily practice with one phrase at a time.

qa.q: What is it like for Yash to watch this change?
qa.a: He teases Santosh about the early noise, but he also sees his friend transformed by something his own family shared, which may make him quietly proud.

grounding: Shows the before, during and after of a teen being deeply inspired by a musician's art and life.

passage: Salma has a crush on the debate captain, and I've watched it take over her whole year. She knows his timetable better than her own. She writes his initials inside her geometry box and covers them with a sticker when anyone looks. Every time he speaks at assembly she grips my arm and whispers, "Usha, he's just so kind." Last week, in the canteen line, I saw him snap at the boy who serves tea because the cup was too full. Salma saw it too. On the way back she said, "He must be really stressed with the finals." I didn't argue. I don't know what's really going on in her head. Maybe she knows he isn't perfect and just doesn't want to know yet.

qa.q: What does Salma write inside her geometry box?
qa.a: She writes the debate captain's initials and hides them under a sticker.

qa.q: Why might Salma have explained away the captain snapping at the tea boy?
qa.a: She has built a flawless picture of him in her head, so she seems to want to protect it and quickly finds an excuse rather than feel disappointed.

qa.q: What could Usha do if she wants to help without hurting Salma?
qa.a: She could stay close and keep listening, and gently ask questions about the real boy rather than lecturing or mocking the crush.

qa.q: How is Usha affected by watching her friend's crush?
qa.a: She feels a bit sidelined and worried, and she is unsure what Salma truly thinks, so she chooses silence over a fight.

grounding: An onlooking friend describes a teen's intense, idealised crush that makes her excuse the boy's flaws.

passage:
Monday: A new boy, Asif, joined Chandrika's evening maths tuition. He dropped his pen, grinned, and said sorry to the whole room. Chandrika decided he had the nicest laugh she had ever heard.

Friday: He messaged the tuition group asking for the chapter notes, and she sent them within ten seconds. He replied, "thanks 🙏". She read that one word so many times she knew the exact shape of the emoji. In bed she planned their whole future, down to the colour of their front door.

Three weeks later: Asif still hadn't returned her notebook. When a quieter girl got a sum wrong, he joked about it loudly. Chandrika felt something sink, then oddly loosen. Walking home, she noticed she hadn't checked her phone once.

qa.q: What did Asif ask the tuition group for on Friday?
qa.a: He asked for the chapter notes.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she planned their whole future in bed?
qa.a: She was swept up in an intense, dreamy crush, building a perfect story from one short thanks.

qa.q: How could an older sister or friend support Chandrika through this?
qa.a: Listen without teasing, let her enjoy the feelings, and gently remind her that people show who they are slowly, over time.

qa.q: What would change if Asif had returned the notebook and been kind to the quieter girl?
qa.a: Chandrika's idealised picture might have lasted longer, and the letdown, when it came, might have come from something else.

grounding: Traces a teen's idealised crush rising fast and then softening as she sees the real person.

passage: "Jomon, sit. You think no one understands? When I was a girl of fifteen, I was certain I would marry the boy who played guitar at the church youth festival. I never spoke to him properly, mind you. I just watched. I learnt his cousin's name so I could find out his birthday. I wrote him long letters I never posted and kept them under my mattress. When he smiled in my direction once, I didn't eat dinner, I was so full of it. Your grandmother kept asking, "Avni, are you ill?" She thought I had a fever. Years later I met him at a wedding. Nice fellow, very ordinary, talked about tyre prices. I laughed all the way home. The feeling was real, mind you. But the boy in my head was mostly me."

qa.q: Where did the boy Avni liked play the guitar?
qa.a: He played at the church youth festival.

qa.q: What does Avni's skipping dinner after one smile suggest about her feelings at fifteen?
qa.a: She was so overwhelmed and excited by a tiny sign of attention that ordinary things like hunger faded; the crush filled her completely.

qa.q: What could Jomon take from Avni's story about a crush of their own?
qa.a: Jomon can feel it without shame, while remembering that the person he admires may be quite different up close. 🙂

qa.q: How might Jomon feel hearing this story from Avni?
qa.a: Jomon might feel less alone and less embarrassed, because someone he respects admits she went through the same intense feelings.

grounding: An elder recalls her own idealised teenage crush to reassure a younger relative.

passage: Francis had rehearsed it for a week. After tuition, near the colony gate, he asked Sunaina if she'd come with him to the farewell. She looked at her shoes and said, gently, that she liked him but only as a friend. He nodded, said "cool, cool," and walked home past the vegetable carts without seeing any of them. In the flat he shut the bathroom door and ran the tap so his mother wouldn't hear. His chest felt crushed, as if the whole building sat on it. At dinner he pushed dal around his plate. His mother didn't ask questions. She just left a cup of cocoa outside his door. Around midnight he texted his cousin, "Can I call?" They talked until two.

qa.q: Where did Francis ask Sunaina to go with him to the farewell?
qa.a: He asked her near the colony gate after tuition.

qa.q: What shows that Francis felt overwhelmed by the rejection?
qa.a: He walked home without noticing anything, cried behind a running tap, felt his chest crushed and could not eat his dinner.

qa.q: How did his mother support him, and why did it help?
qa.a: She did not push him to talk; leaving cocoa by his door showed care while giving him the privacy he clearly wanted.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Sunaina to say no?
qa.a: It was probably uncomfortable for her too; looking at her shoes and speaking gently suggest she cared about not hurting him.

grounding: Shows a teen processing the acute, crushing pain of a romantic rejection in a city home.

passage:
"Sharmila, you haven't come out all day."
"Leave it, Irfan bhaiya."
"Is it the girls from class?"
"They made a new group chat. Without me. I saw the screenshot at lunch. They were planning Saturday."
"Maybe it's a mistake—"
"It's not a mistake! Six years, bhaiya. Six years, and they just... cut me out." Her voice cracked. "I keep thinking I did something. I keep scrolling back to check."
"Okay. Stop scrolling for now. Give me the phone."
"Why?"
"Because you'll read it forty times and feel worse each time. I'll keep it on the table. You can have it back whenever."
A long pause. "It hurts right here." She pressed her ribs.
"I know. Come, walk with me to the milk booth. You don't have to talk."

qa.q: What did Sharmila see at lunch?
qa.a: She saw a screenshot of a new group chat made without her.

qa.q: What is Sharmila worried about as she keeps scrolling back?
qa.a: She fears she did something wrong to be dropped after six years, and she is searching for a reason to make sense of the pain.

qa.q: Why was Irfan's offer to hold the phone a helpful step?
qa.a: It broke the loop of rereading and gave her a pause without taking control, since she could have it back whenever she wanted.

qa.q: What would change if Irfan had said the friends weren't worth crying over?
qa.a: Sharmila might have felt dismissed and pulled further away, because her hurt about six years of friendship would not have been heard. 🫂

grounding: Shows a teen in acute pain after being socially shut out, with a sibling helping her through it.

passage: Shankar ended it by text on a Tuesday night, two lines, polite. I read it standing in the kitchen and forgot I was holding a glass of water until it tipped. For about a week, I was not a person. I deleted all our photos, then panicked and restored them from the bin. I'd be fine in class and then a song in the canteen would make my eyes sting. My sister made me run with her every morning ("Up, Jasleen, shoes on"), which I hated at first. Running was the only time my head went quiet. Looking back now, a couple of months later, I don't hate him. I was just so sure I'd be with him forever. It still pinches when I pass his street, but it doesn't knock the air out of me.

qa.q: How did Shankar end the relationship?
qa.a: He ended it with a polite two-line text on a Tuesday night.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen delete the photos and then restore them?
qa.a: Jasleen was torn between wanting to erase the pain and being afraid to lose the memories, which shows how confused and raw she felt.

qa.q: What helped Jasleen, and why did it work?
qa.a: The morning runs with the sister, because moving quieted the racing thoughts and gave Jasleen a steady routine with someone who cared.

qa.q: How might Jasleen's sister have seen that first week?
qa.a: She probably saw Jasleen hurting and chose a practical way to help, persisting even when Jasleen hated the runs at first.

grounding: A teen looks back on processing the overwhelming pain of a romantic breakup and how it eased.

passage: Lights-out had already gone in the boys' hostel, but Ojas was still sitting on his bed, turning his torch on and off. Kiran looked up from his bunk. "What's with you?" For a long moment Ojas said nothing. Then, very fast: "My parents are separating. Papa moved out last month. I haven't told anyone." His ears went hot. He waited for a joke. Kiran sat up and swung his legs down. "That's heavy, yaar. You've been carrying that alone?" Ojas nodded, eyes on the floor. "I thought you'd think I was weird." "Why would I?" Kiran said. "My uncle and aunty split. It was rough on my cousin." They talked in whispers until the warden's footsteps passed. Ojas slept better that night than he had in weeks.

qa.q: Who moved out last month, according to Ojas?
qa.a: His Papa moved out.

qa.q: What was Ojas afraid of before he spoke?
qa.a: He feared Kiran would mock him or think he was weird, which is why his ears went hot and he waited for a joke.

qa.q: Which reply from Kiran made opening up feel safe, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether Ojas had carried it alone showed he took it seriously, and sharing his cousin's story made Ojas feel less strange.

qa.q: What would change if Kiran had laughed?
qa.a: Ojas would likely have shut down and kept the secret even longer, feeling more alone and less willing to trust anyone.

grounding: Shows a teen taking the risky step of opening up to a peer about something painful, and the relief when it is received well.

passage:
Hi Yash,

Okay, this is weird to write, so I'm just going to type it before I chicken out.

When you asked on the phone last week how the new school was, I said "amazing, everyone's great." That wasn't true. I eat lunch in the library most days. Nobody's mean, I just haven't found my people, and I miss our gang so much it's embarrassing.

I didn't tell you because I thought you'd feel sorry for me, or think I'd become a loser here. But you're my oldest friend, and pretending with you felt worse than being lonely.

So, yeah. That's the truth. You don't have to fix anything. I just didn't want to lie to you anymore.

Your friend (who is fine, just not amazing),
Naveen

qa.q: Where does Naveen eat lunch most days at the new school?
qa.a: In the library, most days.

qa.q: Why did Naveen first tell Yash the school was amazing?
qa.a: Naveen was afraid Yash would feel sorry for Naveen or see Naveen as a loser, so the loneliness stayed hidden.

qa.q: What could Yash do after reading this email?
qa.a: Yash could thank Naveen for being honest, give Naveen a call, and keep in regular touch without rushing to fix things.

qa.q: If you were Yash, how might this email feel?
qa.a: It might sting that Naveen hid the truth, but it would also feel like a gift of trust from an old friend. 🤍

grounding: A teen writes to a close friend, taking the risk of dropping a brave front and admitting loneliness.

passage: "So, Simran, you asked about the hardest thing I did this year. It wasn't boards. It was one evening at Sneha's terrace. All my friends were talking about the trip to the hills, and I kept saying I'd 'check dates.' Truth was, my dad had lost his job in March and there was no money for trips. I'd been pretending for months: new excuses, fake busy. That evening I just... said it. My hands were shaking. I said, 'Guys, I can't afford it, and I've been lying because I was ashamed.' Nobody spoke for a second. Then Sneha said, 'Rukmini, why didn't you tell us?' and someone suggested a picnic at the lake instead. I cried a bit on the way home, but lighter, you know?"

qa.q: What had happened to Rukmini's dad in March?
qa.a: He had lost his job.

qa.q: How can you tell that telling the friends felt risky for Rukmini?
qa.a: Rukmini's hands were shaking, and Rukmini admits to months of shame and excuses.

qa.q: What could Rukmini's friends keep doing to support Rukmini?
qa.a: They could keep choosing low-cost plans like the lake picnic and check in quietly, without making money the centre of every talk.

qa.q: How might Sneha have felt when Rukmini spoke up?
qa.a: Sneha seems surprised and a little hurt that a friend carried this alone, but eager to help, asking why Rukmini hadn't told them.

grounding: A teen recounts opening up to friends about a hidden family hardship and how it deepened the friendship.

passage:
"Parul, you've read the same page for twenty minutes."
"Didi, I can't breathe properly. Tomorrow's physics paper and I don't remember anything."
"Okay, put the book down. Look at me. Breathe in slowly through your nose."
"This is silly—"
"Humour me. In... now out, even slower, like you're cooling hot tea."
"...Okay."
"Again. Drop your shoulders. They're up near your ears."
"My heart's still going fast."
"That's fine. It'll slow. Now shoes on. We're walking round the building twice."
"Nikita didi, I don't have time!"
"You don't have time to panic either. Ten minutes outside, then back to the book."
Later, climbing the stairs, Parul said, "My head feels less jammed."
"Good. Do that breathing in the exam hall if it starts again. 🙂"

qa.q: How many times did Nikita want to walk round the building?
qa.a: Nikita wanted them to walk round the building twice.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling before Nikita stepped in?
qa.a: Parul was panicking about the physics paper, struggling to breathe properly and sure of remembering nothing.

qa.q: What small step did Nikita suggest for the exam hall itself?
qa.a: She suggested using the same slow breathing if the panic started again during the paper.

qa.q: How does Nikita see Parul's protest about having no time?
qa.a: She sees that panic is wasting more time than a short walk would, so she calmly insists on the break.

grounding: Shows a teen using slow breathing and a brisk walk, coached by Nikita didi, to handle exam anxiety.

passage: Last term I had to present our science project in front of the whole school. The night before, my stomach felt like it was full of wasps. I kept rehearsing in the mirror and getting worse. Afreen called and I told her I might fake a cold. She said, "Jaya, go run. Seriously." So I jogged up and down our lane until my legs burned, then lay on the floor and breathed out long and slow, the way our PE teacher taught us. It didn't magic the fear away, but I slept. Next morning, backstage, my hands went cold again. I pressed my feet into the floor and counted my breaths. My voice shook for the first minute and then it didn't. I finished. People clapped.

qa.q: Who suggested that Jaya go for a run?
qa.a: Afreen did, when she called and said, 'Go run.'

qa.q: What does Jaya's thought of faking a cold show about Jaya's state the night before?
qa.a: Jaya was so anxious that avoiding the presentation felt like the only escape, with a stomach full of wasps and rehearsing only making it worse.

qa.q: Which strategies helped Jaya, and why did they work?
qa.a: Running, slow breathing and pressing her feet into the floor helped because they calmed Jaya's body enough to sleep and to get past the shaky first minute.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel hearing that Jaya finished and people clapped?
qa.a: She would likely feel glad and a bit proud, since her blunt advice helped her friend face the fear instead of hiding. 😊

grounding: A teen recalls handling intense performance anxiety with exercise, breathwork and grounding.

passage:
Coach's note, inter-school chess final, Saturday.

Before round three, Lokesh came to me pale, rubbing his palms on his trousers. He said his mind had gone "blank white" and that his parents had taken the day off to watch. I did not tell him to relax. I asked him to sit, press both feet flat on the floor, and breathe out longer than he breathed in, several times. Then we walked once around the corridor, and I asked him to name five things he could see.

He went back in with steadier hands. He lost the game, but played carefully and did not rush his moves, which is where he usually slips.

Next step: I will practise this routine with the whole team during Tuesday practice, not just before finals. — Jagdish

qa.q: What did Lokesh say had happened to his mind before round three?
qa.a: He said his mind had gone blank white.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have been worried about, based on the note?
qa.a: He seemed afraid of letting his parents down, since they had taken the day off to watch him in the final.

qa.q: Why is the coach's plan to practise the routine on Tuesdays wise?
qa.a: Calming habits work best when they are practised in ordinary moments, so the whole team can reach for them automatically under pressure.

qa.q: What would change if the coach had simply said 'just relax'?
qa.a: Lokesh would probably have felt unheard and stayed tense, because being told to relax gives no concrete way to calm the body.

grounding: A coach records a teen using grounding, slow exhaling and movement to manage competition anxiety.

passage: Jamal stood at the lockers in his school in Leeds, holding the new notice: students who missed two homework deadlines would lose the end-of-year trip. "That's not fair," he told Esther. "Dev looks after his little brothers every evening. He misses homework because of that, not laziness." Esther shrugged. "Rules are rules." "But why is it a rule?" Jamal said. "What's it for? To make us learn, or to punish?" He went quiet, then frowned. "Although if they make exceptions for everyone, the teachers can't run anything." He chewed his pen through maths, sketching arguments on the back of his notebook. By lunch he had drafted a short letter to the head of year asking for a way to explain missed work privately, instead of scrapping the rule entirely.

qa.q: What would students lose for missing two homework deadlines?
qa.a: They would lose the end-of-year trip.

qa.q: What does Jamal's frowning and chewing his pen suggest about what's going on inside him?
qa.a: He is genuinely torn: he feels the rule is unfair to Dev but also sees that teachers need some rules, so he is working out what he actually believes.

qa.q: Why was asking for a private way to explain missed work a sensible choice?
qa.a: It keeps the purpose of the rule while protecting students with real reasons, so it is more likely to be heard than a demand to scrap it.

qa.q: Why might Esther react differently to the notice than Jamal?
qa.a: She may see rules as simply there to follow, while Jamal is thinking about a friend's situation and what the rule is meant to achieve.

grounding: Shows a teen questioning a rule that seems arbitrary and weighing competing values to shape his own view of fairness.

passage: At the girls' hostel meeting, the warden repeated the rule: girls inside by seven, boys' block by nine. Vinita raised her hand. "Ma'am, why two different times? We have the same classes." A few seniors went still. The warden said it was for safety. "Then isn't the answer better lights near the gate, not locking us in?" Vinita asked. Her voice wobbled, but she kept going. Later, Dhruv from the boys' block messaged her: "Brave. But you'll get a black mark." She lay awake. Was she being disrespectful to someone who truly worried about them? Or was staying silent the real wrong? By morning she had decided: she'd keep asking, politely, and collect signatures for the lighting request instead of just complaining.

qa.q: What time did the rule say the girls had to be inside?
qa.a: The girls had to be inside by seven.

qa.q: Why was Vinita unsure she had done the right thing as she lay awake?
qa.a: She wondered whether questioning the warden was disrespectful to someone who cared about their safety, or whether keeping quiet about an unfair rule was the bigger wrong.

qa.q: What made Vinita's final plan a thoughtful one?
qa.a: She kept her challenge respectful and practical, asking for better lighting with signatures, which addresses safety instead of just attacking the rule.

qa.q: How does Dhruv see what Vinita did?
qa.a: He admires her courage but worries it will get her into trouble, so his message mixes praise and warning.

grounding: A teen in a hostel challenges a norm that seems arbitrary and works through the ethical tension to choose her stance.

passage:
Dear Tenzin,

Something happened and I need to think it through with someone who won't just give me a lecture.

In the chemistry test, I saw my friend Meghna copying from notes under her desk. You know her parents: if she fails, home becomes a war zone. Part of me thinks, who am I to report her? Another part thinks it isn't fair to everyone who studied till midnight, including me.

I used to believe cheating was simply wrong, full stop. Now I see it's tangled. Being loyal matters to me. So does honesty. They're pulling in opposite directions.

I think I'm going to talk to Meghna first, not the teacher. Tell her I saw, and that I won't cover for her if it happens again. Is that a cop-out?

Write back soon,
Reena

qa.q: What did Reena see Meghna doing during the chemistry test?
qa.a: She saw Meghna copying from notes under her desk.

qa.q: Why does Reena feel pulled in two directions?
qa.a: Reena feels torn between loyalty to Meghna, whose home life is hard, and honesty and fairness to the students who studied.

qa.q: What would you advise Reena about her plan?
qa.a: Talking to Meghna first is a fair step; she could also suggest Meghna seek help from a teacher so the pressure does not push her to cheat again.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He is likely to feel trusted, since Reena chose him because he won't lecture, and he may think carefully about how to answer her honest question.

grounding: A teen writes about a real ethical dilemma, wrestling with conflicting values to define her own moral stance.

passage: The morning bus from the village to the kasba school was always packed. Tushar sat near the back, as usual, while a group of older boys copied the way he stammered on his name. Some girls giggled. Urmila, squeezed by the window with her tiffin on her lap, felt her face go hot. Her cousin was among the boys. If she said anything, it would reach every house in the village by evening. The bus jolted past the sugarcane fields. Tushar stared at his knees. Urmila stood up, walked down the swaying aisle and sat beside him. "Enough," she said loudly. "Would you like it done to you?" Her cousin rolled his eyes and muttered something. The boys went quiet, a little sulky. Tushar didn't say a word, but he moved his bag so she had room.

qa.q: Where was the bus going?
qa.a: It was going from the village to the kasba school.

qa.q: Why did Urmila hesitate before speaking up?
qa.a: She feared the social cost, since her cousin was one of the teasers and gossip would spread through the village by evening.

qa.q: How could a teacher support what Urmila started?
qa.a: A teacher could quietly check in with Tushar, speak to the older boys about the teasing, and back Urmila so she isn't left facing the backlash alone.

qa.q: How might Tushar have experienced Urmila sitting beside him?
qa.a: After feeling humiliated, he probably felt less alone and protected; moving his bag suggests quiet gratitude.

grounding: A teen in a small-town setting defends a teased peer even though it risks trouble with her own cousin and neighbours.

passage: In the cafeteria of a high school in Toronto, Soo-ah opened her lunch box of kimbap, and a boy at the next table held his nose and laughed. His friends joined in. Camila, who usually sat with the popular crowd by the windows, watched Soo-ah quietly close the lid. Camila's stomach turned. She picked up her tray, walked across the room and sat opposite Soo-ah. "That looks amazing. Can I try one? I'll trade you my crackers." Soo-ah blinked, then slid the box over. The window table went silent, then someone snorted. Over the next week, Camila wasn't invited to a birthday party she'd assumed she'd be at. It stung. But she kept sitting with Soo-ah, and by Friday two others had joined them.

qa.q: What did Camila offer Soo-ah in exchange?
qa.a: She offered to trade her crackers for one of the kimbap.

qa.q: What does Camila's turning stomach suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She was upset and uncomfortable watching Soo-ah being mocked, which pushed her to act.

qa.q: What did it cost Camila to stand by Soo-ah, and why was it still worth it?
qa.a: She lost an invitation to a party and some status, but she stayed loyal to what felt right and it gave Soo-ah company.

qa.q: How might the popular group see Camila's choice?
qa.a: Some may feel embarrassed or annoyed at being shown up, which could explain the snort and the missing invitation.

grounding: Shows a teen defending a mocked peer at a social cost and sticking with that choice.

passage: "Damini didi, you know when Nanu died last winter? Everyone kept telling me, 'Darshan, he's in a better place,' and I kept thinking, how do they know? I wasn't angry exactly. Just... it cracked something open. Where did he go? Does anything I do matter if we all end? I started reading at night, anything I could find: old stories from the Upanishads, a book on black holes, even Nanu's own diary in Gujarati, which took ages. I sat in the temple some evenings and in the library some afternoons. I don't have answers. Some days that scares me. Other days it feels exciting, like I'm allowed to decide what I believe instead of just copying. Is that weird? You're the only one I can say this to."

qa.q: Whose diary did Darshan read?
qa.a: Nanu's own diary, written in Gujarati.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Darshan describe about not having answers?
qa.a: Some days the uncertainty scares Darshan, while on other days it feels exciting because Darshan gets to decide what he believes.

qa.q: What could Damini say to support Darshan?
qa.a: She could tell Darshan these questions are normal and worth having, listen without rushing to answers, and maybe share what she herself wonders about.

qa.q: How might Darshan's parents feel if they knew about the reading?
qa.a: They might be moved that Darshan is honouring Nanu, or uneasy about the questioning of what the family says, depending on how they see such doubts.

grounding: A teen tells an older didi how a loss started a search for meaning, faith and a personal philosophy.

passage: Sahil used to be the loudest one on our cricket team, always joking. This year Pankaj, that's me, noticed he'd changed. In physics, when Sir mentioned the universe was expanding, Sahil asked, "Expanding into what?" and then, "Why is there anything at all?" The class laughed. He didn't. After school he started staying back in the library with thick books from the philosophy shelf. On Sundays I saw him at the gurdwara, not just eating langar like before but serving it, quiet and focused. Once I asked him if something was wrong. He said, "No, I just want to know what I'm for." I didn't really get it. I still don't know if he's happy or worried. But he seems more awake than before, like he's listening for something.

qa.q: What did Sahil ask when the physics teacher said the universe was expanding?
qa.a: He asked what it was expanding into, and then why there is anything at all.

qa.q: What does Sahil's reply, 'I just want to know what I'm for,' suggest about his mind?
qa.a: He seems curious and searching for purpose, taking big questions about his place in the world seriously rather than as a joke.

qa.q: How could the physics teacher encourage Sahil's questions?
qa.a: He could welcome them, point him to readable books, or give time after class to talk, instead of letting the class laugh them away.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see his friend's change?
qa.a: He is puzzled and unsure whether Sahil is happy or worried, but he notices Sahil seems more awake and focused.

grounding: A friend observes a teen exploring deep questions of existence and purpose through study and spiritual practice.

passage:
First Sunday: Jasleen stood through the morning prayer at the gurdwara, thinking mostly about her maths test, the words washing past her like traffic.

The next Thursday: On a school visit to an old-age home, an old man with shaky hands held hers and asked, "Beta, what are you living for?" She laughed nervously. She had no answer. On the bus back she stared out of the window, the question stuck in her ribs.

A month later: Her notebook was titled "Things I Believe (So Far)". It had bits of Gurbani, a line from a science book about atoms made in stars, and crossed-out pages. Shankar, who called himself an atheist, argued with her at recess. "You can't prove any of it." "Maybe not," she said. "But I'm allowed to look."

qa.q: What was the title of Jasleen's notebook a month later?
qa.a: It was titled 'Things I Believe (So Far)'.

qa.q: Why did the old man's question stay with Jasleen?
qa.a: She realised she had never thought about her purpose, and not having an answer unsettled her and made her want to search.

qa.q: What small step helped Jasleen explore these questions?
qa.a: Keeping a notebook where she could collect ideas from faith and science, and cross things out as her thinking changed.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Jasleen's search?
qa.a: As an atheist he doubts her ideas can be proven, but by arguing at recess he is also taking her questions seriously.

grounding: Shows over several weeks a teen moving from routine ritual to actively exploring meaning, belief and purpose.

passage: Every Saturday Kamal and Gopika taught English and maths to children of the construction workers behind their school, under a tin shed the site manager let them use. This Saturday, the rain came down so hard the shed roof began to drip onto the chalk slates. Twelve kids and nowhere dry. Gopika wanted to cancel. Kamal looked at the children huddled together, a few still in wet uniforms. "They walked here in this," he said. They borrowed a tarp from the watchman, tied it over the leaking corner, and moved everyone to the dry side. Kamal taught fractions by splitting rotis a mother had sent. When one girl said her old school teacher had called her "dirty", Kamal quietly told her, "Here, you're our best maths student."

qa.q: What did Kamal use to teach fractions?
qa.a: He used rotis a mother had sent.

qa.q: Why did Kamal refuse to cancel even though the shed was leaking?
qa.a: He felt responsible to the children, who had walked through the rain to come, and he did not want to let them down.

qa.q: What did Kamal do well when the girl mentioned being called dirty?
qa.a: He quietly countered the insult with respect, naming her strength so she felt valued rather than judged.

qa.q: How might Gopika's view have changed after the rainy session?
qa.a: She first wanted to cancel, but seeing the tarp work and the children learning may have shown her how much showing up matters.

grounding: Shows teens devoting weekends to a cause and standing up for marginalised children despite a practical obstacle.

passage: When Saurabh joined Class 10 on a scholarship, the others noticed his old shoes and the way he took the bus from the far end of the city. At lunch he ate alone near the water cooler. Kiran noticed too. At first she did nothing. Then one day she overheard two boys calling him "charity case". Her face burned. That afternoon she carried her tiffin to the water cooler and asked Saurabh about the chess book he was reading. By Friday, three more friends were eating there. Kiran also signed up for Sunday mornings at the community kitchen near the railway station, where she stirred huge pots of khichdi. Her mother asked why. "Because I'm tired of just noticing things," Kiran said, stirring harder.

qa.q: Where did Kiran volunteer on Sunday mornings?
qa.a: At the community kitchen near the railway station.

qa.q: What made Kiran decide to act instead of just noticing?
qa.a: Hearing the boys call Saurabh a charity case made her angry and ashamed of doing nothing, so she felt she had to step in.

qa.q: How could a class teacher support what Kiran began?
qa.a: The teacher could arrange mixed seating or group work so Saurabh is included naturally, and speak to the boys about the name-calling.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh when Kiran sits with him?
qa.a: After eating alone and being mocked, having someone ask about his chess book likely makes him feel seen as a person, not a label.

grounding: Shows a teen turning concern into action through volunteering and including an excluded classmate.

passage:
"Amma, Irfan and I want to start a petition."
"For what now?"
"A ramp. Nisha from our class uses a wheelchair and she has to wait for two boys to lift her up the science block stairs."
"Doesn't the school know?"
"They say there's no budget. Irfan found the board rules. Schools are meant to be accessible."
"And your exams?"
"Amma, it's one hour a day. Irfan's making the form, I'm getting signatures."
Irfan, from the doorway: "Aunty, we asked Nisha first. She wants it. We're not doing it for her without asking."
"Hmm. That's sensible." A pause. "Lakshmi, don't be rude to the principal."
"I'll be polite. Promise."
"Fine. Give me the form. I'll sign too."

qa.q: Why does Nisha have to wait at the science block?
qa.a: She uses a wheelchair and has to wait for two boys to lift her up the stairs.

qa.q: What might Amma be worried about at first?
qa.a: She seems worried the petition will eat into Lakshmi's exam preparation and that Lakshmi may be rude to the principal.

qa.q: Which choice by Irfan and Lakshmi was especially wise, and why?
qa.a: Asking Nisha first made sure they were supporting what she actually wanted, rather than speaking over her.

qa.q: What would change if they had started without talking to Nisha?
qa.a: The campaign might embarrass her or not match her needs, and she could feel like a project instead of a classmate.

grounding: Shows teens committing to a cause for a marginalised peer and convincing a parent while balancing studies.

passage:
Karthik: bro everyone's going to the quarry tonight. jumping off the ledge 🤩
Baljeet: the flooded one? isn't it deep and dark
Karthik: that's the point lol. Arjun did it last week
Karthik: if I don't go they'll call me scared again
Baljeet: ok but it's midnight and nobody can see the rocks
Karthik: you sound like my mom
Baljeet: fine. but you're typing like 100 words a min. you ok?
Karthik: I'm just hyped
Karthik: also kinda annoyed they laughed at me at practice
Baljeet: so this is about that?
Karthik: ...maybe
Baljeet: what if you say you'll come in the daytime on Sunday. see it properly
Karthik: they'll say I'm chickening out
Baljeet: let them. we'll go together in daylight
Karthik: ok. yeah. sleeping instead 😴

qa.q: Where was everyone planning to go that night?
qa.a: To the flooded quarry to jump off the ledge.

qa.q: What feeling does Karthik admit is really pushing the plan to go?
qa.a: Karthik is annoyed that the others laughed at practice and wants to prove not being scared, so hurt pride and excitement are driving the choice.

qa.q: What worked in how Baljeet helped Karthik decide?
qa.a: Baljeet noticed Karthik's rush, asked about the real feeling behind it, and offered a calmer daytime option together instead of just saying no.

qa.q: How might the group see Karthik if he skips tonight?
qa.a: Some may tease Karthik for chickening out, but that teasing is exactly the pressure Baljeet helps Karthik see past.

grounding: Shows a teen, with a friend's help, slowing down a risky choice driven by excitement, hurt pride and peer pressure.

passage: At the Dussehra mela in their kasba, the older boys crowded around Bhupen's uncle's motorbike. "Divyansh, take a round," one said, tossing him the keys. "Just to the canal and back." Divyansh's heart pounded. He was sixteen and had no licence, and he'd only ever ridden it slowly in the courtyard. The boys started chanting his name. His hand closed on the keys. Then Bhupen caught his eye and gave a tiny shake of the head. Divyansh said, "Wait, let me get a chai first," and walked to the stall, away from the noise. He sipped, watched the crowded road and the tractor lights. By the time he came back, his hands were steady. He handed the keys back. "Not today." A couple of boys booed. He shrugged and went to the giant wheel.

qa.q: Where did the boys want Divyansh to ride the motorbike to?
qa.a: To the canal and back.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when the boys started chanting his name?
qa.a: He was excited and under intense pressure, with a pounding heart, and part of him wanted to prove himself.

qa.q: Why was stepping away for chai a smart move?
qa.a: It gave him a few minutes away from the chanting to calm down and see the crowded road clearly before deciding.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see the situation?
qa.a: He seems worried, since it is his uncle's bike and the road is crowded, and his small head shake signals that he hopes Divyansh will say no.

grounding: Shows a teen cooling down in a heated moment of peer pressure before making a safer choice.

passage: In her bedroom in Dublin, Dalia got a text from Liam: "You told everyone about my parents?? Thanks a lot." She hadn't. Her face went hot. Her thumbs flew across the screen: "Are you serious?? I'd NEVER do that, you're paranoid and honestly exhausting." Her finger hovered over send. She remembered last spring, when she'd sent something similar to a friend and they hadn't spoken for months. She put the phone face down on the bed, went downstairs and made toast she didn't really want. She texted her cousin a rant instead. Twenty minutes later, she deleted her draft and wrote: "I didn't tell anyone. I'm upset you'd think that. Can we talk tomorrow?" Liam replied the next morning: "Sorry. Someone else said it was you."

qa.q: What did Liam accuse Dalia of in his text?
qa.a: He accused her of telling everyone about his parents.

qa.q: What made Dalia pause before sending her first reply?
qa.a: She remembered how a similar angry message last spring cost her a friendship for months.

qa.q: What could Dalia try again the next time she feels that heat?
qa.a: Put the phone away and do something ordinary until the anger settles, then write a calm message that states her feelings.

qa.q: How might things have gone for Liam if Dalia had sent the first draft?
qa.a: He would have felt attacked while already upset about his parents, and the misunderstanding could have become a long falling-out.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing her emotional heat and delaying a reply to make a cooler, wiser choice.
